titleText.es: Nunca volveré a comprar un aire acondicionado con mi administrador de sistemas.
titleText.en: I am never going out to buy an air-conditioner with my sysadmin again.
titleText.noteEn: The title text extends the joke about turning an ordinary purchase into a prolonged technical analysis.

Ir names physical going, a links it to the purpose action, and comprar stays in its dictionary form.

applications.explanationEn: Sale supplies the changing form of salir, más strengthens the value comparison, and a cuenta completes the fixed expression.
Qué tal asks for an opinion, and ese supplies the masculine option being considered.

applications.explanationEn: Nos names the people affected, sale supplies the changing verb, más makes the comparison, and a cuenta completes the fixed expression.
Dos horas gives the duration, and después follows it to place the next moment that amount of time later.

regions.labelEs: CREO QUE NUESTRO PRINCIPAL PROBLEMA ES NUESTRA DEFINICIÓN POCO CLARA DE VALOR.

applications.explanationEn: Vuestro addresses more than one person informally and matches the masculine singular thing possessed.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.promptEs: ir a + infinitivo · movimiento con propósito
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone physically goes to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes for the person and time, while the final action stays in the dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Context can make this pattern describe real movement toward an activity, rather than the separate near-future meaning “going to do.”

example.en: We went to get bread.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)

cards.noteEn: Malo names the negative quality being evaluated. In ¿qué tiene de malo?, the complete question asks what is wrong or bad about something.

example.es: No veo nada malo en la idea.
example.en: I do not see anything wrong with the idea.

cards.answerEn: non-; not a (before a category label)
cards.noteEn: Before a noun used as a label, no can divide people or things into a negative category, much like English non-. It remains a separate written word.

example.es: La entrada para no miembros está cerrada.
example.en: The entrance for non-members is closed.

cards.noteEn: Cerebritos is the plural of cerebrito, a playful or mocking label for highly intellectual people rather than a literal reference to small brains.

example.en: The brainiacs solved the puzzle.

cards.noteEn: Cerebrito literally resembles “little brain,” but it is commonly a playful or mocking label for a very intellectual person. Tone decides whether it sounds affectionate or insulting.

example.es: Mi hermano es un cerebrito de las matemáticas.
example.en: My brother is a math brainiac.

cards.noteEn: Pillemos is a “we” proposal form of pillar, an informal verb that can mean “to get” or “to grab.” The -emos ending turns pillar into a suggestion for the group.

example.en: Let's get a taxi.

cards.promptEs: propuesta para nosotros: hablemos, comamos, vivamos
cards.questionEn: How do you propose an action for a group that includes yourself, like “let's talk”?
cards.answerEn: Use the special “we” proposal form: most -ar verbs take -emos, while most -er and -ir verbs take -amos.
cards.noteEn: Start from the verb's dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Hablar becomes hablemos, comer becomes comamos, and vivir becomes vivamos. Some verbs also change their spelling or base, so learn unfamiliar forms as you meet them.

example.en: Let's look for another table.

cards.noteEn: When ese appears without a following noun, it stands in for a masculine singular thing already visible or understood.

example.en: I prefer that one.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: is worthwhile; works out as good value (as part of salir a cuenta)
cards.noteEn: Sale normally comes from salir, “to go out,” but in salir a cuenta it describes whether a choice works out as worthwhile or good value.

example.es: El pase mensual sale a cuenta.
example.en: The monthly pass is worthwhile.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a choice is worthwhile or works out as better value for someone?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of salir followed by a cuenta. Add más for “better value,” and place me, te, le, nos, os, or les before salir when naming who benefits.
cards.noteEn: This is a fixed use of salir; translating it as “to go out” would be misleading. Salir changes for the thing being evaluated, while a cuenta stays fixed. The short word before salir identifies the person affected, if one is stated.

example.es: Nos sale más a cuenta el abono mensual.
example.en: The monthly pass works out as better value for us.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of salir a cuenta
cards.noteEn: This a is required inside the fixed expression salir a cuenta, meaning that something works out as worthwhile or good value.

example.es: Comprar el paquete sale a cuenta.
example.en: Buying the package is worthwhile.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes salir a cuenta, “to be worthwhile”
cards.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account or a bill elsewhere. In salir a cuenta, the whole expression evaluates whether something is advantageous or good value.

example.es: El billete de ida y vuelta sale a cuenta.
example.en: The round-trip ticket is good value.

cards.answerEn: how (as part of qué tal, “how about...?”)
cards.noteEn: In qué tal, qué keeps its accent and joins tal to ask for an opinion or propose an option. Translate the two words together rather than assigning qué its ordinary “what” meaning by itself.

example.en: How about this table?

cards.questionEn: How do you ask for an opinion about an option or suggest it for consideration?
cards.answerEn: Use ¿qué tal...? before or around the option, much like “how about...?”
cards.noteEn: Qué keeps its written accent in the question. Tal completes this fixed expression, and the option can be a noun, a pronoun such as ese, or a time such as mañana.

example.en: How about Friday?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes qué tal, “how about...?”
cards.noteEn: Tal completes qué tal, a common expression used to ask how something is or to suggest an option. It does not have a useful separate English translation in this expression.

example.en: How about tomorrow?

cards.noteEn: Before a verb such as salir or resultar, nos can identify the people for whom an outcome is advantageous, costly, easy, or difficult.

example.es: Nos resulta más barato viajar juntos.
example.en: It works out cheaper for us to travel together.

cards.answerEn: I am (in a state or condition)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens a stated amount of time later?
cards.answerEn: Put the length of time before después.
cards.noteEn: The duration comes first: tres días después means “three days later.” This differs from después de tres días, which presents the same duration after después and means “after three days.”

example.es: Tres días después, llegó la carta.
example.en: Three days later, the letter arrived.

cards.noteEn: Principal identifies the most important or central one. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: This is the main entrance.

cards.noteEn: Before a describing word, poco often says that a quality is present to an insufficient degree. Poco claro therefore means “not very clear,” while un poco claro would literally mean “a little clear.”

example.en: The sign is not very visible.

cards.answerEn: your (informal plural, before a masculine singular noun)

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.
